newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - NatWest to raise pre-excep profit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - NatWest to raise pre-excep profit.

text.p: National Westminster Bank Plc will announce a rise in pre-tax profits before exceptional items on Tuesday and the market is also expecting it to repurchase some shares.
After the exceptionals and disposal losses, NatWest is expected to post a pre-tax profit of between 1.09 billion stg and 1.25 billion stg with several analysts having cut their estimates.
Most of the adjustments to NatWest's figures come from the first half where there were large disposal losses associated with the sale of its U.S. retail unit Bancorp.
Robert Law, Lehman Brothers' banking analyst, is forecasting pre-exceptional profits up eight percent at 1.89 billion stg and a stated profit of 1.195 billion stg.
NatWest is expected to pay a dividend per share in the region of 29p after 25.3p in 1995.
The bank has authority from shareholders to buy back a further 28 million shares, which would cost around 225 million stg at current prices, after it spent 450 million stg on a buy-back last August.
As far as the bank's performance is concerned, the benign domestic economic conditions bode well for NatWest UK which will also see its costs continuing to fall.
But the group's investment banking arm, NatWest Markets, could be a disappointment if its equivalent at Barclays, BZW, is anything to go by.

BZW saw profits dip by nearly 30 percent in 1996 and although NatWest Markets has not seen the upheavals in management that BZW has experienced, it is trying to integrate some important acquisitions such as Greenwich Capital and Hambro Magan.
It is likely that NatWest executives will face similar questions to those put to Barclays. When will the returns from the investment banking operation justify the investment and upheaval?
Did NatWest choose exactly the wrong time in the business cycle to expand NatWest Markets? And will the UK bank continue to be able to subsidise that expansion?
